title: Grid-Scale Battery Storage — Competitive Assessment
topic: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems — the head-to-head set of system suppliers and integrators

scope.rationale: 12 covered companies selling grid-scale BESS at system level — cell-to-system suppliers and pure integrators; component-only and power-electronics players excluded

gaps: All revenue comparisons are **whole-company**, not BESS-segment — segment splits are not comparably disclosed across the twelve. A company-level figure overstates BESS scale for diversified groups (storage is a single-digit share of BYD and Tesla revenue) and is the whole business only for pure plays like Fluence.
Hithium’s comparable figure is FY2024, from its HKEX listing prospectus [c:c23] — no FY2025 full-year figure is publicly filed.

FlexGen is private with no disclosed revenue; Wärtsilä’s storage-unit revenue is not separable from the group ahead of the announced JV [c:c37]. Both appear without comparable figures rather than with manufactured ones.
Dossiers were last updated 2026-08-22/24 — before the Sungrow and BYD H1 2026 reports scheduled for 2026-08-29.

bluf: The competitive center of grid-scale BESS sits with vertically integrated Chinese cell-owners — Sungrow took Wood Mackenzie’s inaugural comprehensive integrator ranking from Tesla [c:c1], with CATL, BYD and EVE owning the cell cost curve — while the non-Chinese field’s one structural wedge is US domestic content, which Tesla, Fluence, LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are converting into US factories and multi-GWh backlog [c:c7][c:c32][c:c29]. The frontier fight is architectural: maximum single-block density (BYD’s 14.5 MWh HaoHan [c:c17]) versus standardized mass manufacture (Tesla’s ~5 MWh Megapack 3 and 20 MWh Megablock [c:c5]).

keyJudgments.text: We assess that scale leadership sits with the vertically integrated Chinese cell-owners. Sungrow holds the #1 spot in Wood Mackenzie’s inaugural comprehensive global BESS integrator ranking (2026, assessing 2025) — the first vendor to displace Tesla — while CATL, BYD and EVE own the cell cost curve beneath the system market: CATL reported FY2025 revenue of RMB 423.7B with storage its fastest-growing line, and EVE shipped 71.05 GWh of ESS cells (+41%) in FY2025.

We assess the platform race has split into two deliberate architectures: maximum single-block density — BYD’s 14.5 MWh HaoHan (the largest single DC block, on a 2,710 Ah cell), Sungrow’s PowerTitan 3.0 family, Hithium’s 6.25–6.9 MWh ∞Power — versus standardized mass manufacture — Tesla’s ~5 MWh Megapack 3 with the 20 MWh Megablock as the site building brick, and Fluence’s Smartstack skid extended to 10 MWh in the same footprint. The bets differ on where the constraint lies: land and balance-of-plant for the density camp, factory cost and delivery velocity for the standardization camp.

We assess US domestic content is the non-Chinese field’s one structural wedge, and it is being converted into hard backlog: Tesla shipped its first Megapacks on US-made LFP cells and started Megapack 3 production at the 50 GWh/yr Brookshire plant; LG Energy Solution took the $4.3B Megapack 3 LFP cell award and Vertech’s 6 GWh DTE order; Samsung SDI booked over KRW 2T of US LFP ESS on SBB 2.0 against a shrinking EV book.

We assess demand is not the binding constraint — execution is. Fluence cut FY2026 guidance to $2.9–3.1B on production-ramp delays while holding a record $6.4B backlog and $1.44B quarterly intake; Canadian Solar shipped a record 7.8 GWh of storage in FY2025 and still lost $104M; Samsung SDI’s first operating profit in seven quarters came from AI-data-center UPS/BBU demand rather than grid storage. 2026 is being decided on margin and manufacturing ramps, not order books.

We assess the pure-integrator tier is consolidating. Wärtsilä is exiting — storage reclassified as discontinued operations pending a 50/50 JV with RCT Solutions — while the remaining independents reposition on software, services and compliance: FlexGen on hardware-agnostic controls and a services roll-up, Fluence on domestic content plus hyperscaler master supply agreements. Confidence is moderate because the direction is clear but the pace and the next specific exit are not.

sections.title: The Competitive Read
ps: The middle of this market is the dangerous place. The Chinese cell-owners compete from the cost curve down — cells fund systems, systems pull cells — while the compliance camp competes from regulation up, converting FEOC rules and tariffs into US factories and awards. Caught between the camps, a Western player without its own cells ships record volume at a loss (Canadian Solar: 7.8 GWh shipped, a $104M net loss [c:c34]) or holds a record backlog it cannot yet convert (Fluence [c:c10]). Owning either the cell or the compliance story is what separates margin from momentum.

The architecture split is a strategic fork, not marketing. The density camp (BYD, Sungrow, Hithium, CATL) optimizes land, balance-of-plant and per-site economics — the binding constraint in siting-limited markets. The standardization camp (Tesla, Fluence) optimizes the factory — cost, cadence, and delivery certainty at 50 GWh/yr scale [c:c6]. If interconnection queues stay the bottleneck, standardization wins on speed-to-energization; if land and siting dominate, density wins. Neither camp can cheaply switch: the bet is baked into cell format, enclosure, and manufacturing line.

Software and services are where the integrators without cells are retreating to — and it may be the more defensible ground. FlexGen has effectively completed the pivot (hardware-agnostic HybridOS plus a field-services roll-up [c:c36]), Fluence monetizes rivals’ hardware through Mosaic, Tesla couples Autobidder to its own blocks, and Wärtsilä’s GEMS delivery record is the asset its JV partner is buying into [c:c37]. As hardware commoditizes toward Chinese cell pricing, the control-and-optimization layer holds margin the blocks no longer do.

sections.title: The AI Data-Center Adjacency
sections.read: The demand engine pulling this head-to-head into new territory
ps: The dossiers record the BESS field converging on AI data-center power from four directions at once: Fluence put Smartstack into a Siemens/NVIDIA AI-facility reference architecture [c:c40]; Canadian Solar booked a 2.5 GWh order explicitly framed as US data-center power demand [c:c41]; EVE showed a full-matrix BBU portfolio for 800V HVDC racks at OCP China [c:c22]; and Samsung SDI’s entire profit recovery is UPS/BBU-led [c:c27]. Grid-scale storage and data-center power — covered as separate spaces in this app — are becoming one buyer conversation.

limitations: Comparisons are whole-company revenue, not BESS-segment revenue — segment disclosure is not comparable across the twelve (see the coverage gaps).
Shipment and share rankings (Wood Mackenzie, SNE/InfoLink) are independent-analyst estimates reproduced as the dossiers cite them — not re-verified for this report.

This report is built from the covered dossiers alone: no fresh research was performed, and no field-note content appears in it. Sourcing quality is therefore bounded by each dossier’s own source list — per-company first-party shares are shown under Coverage.
Collection gap: Hithium FY2025 full-year results are not publicly filed (lapsed HKEX listings); FlexGen discloses no financials; Wärtsilä’s storage unit is not separately reported ahead of the JV.
